title: What grabbed him as a kid: his father's piano and the family's music
summary: Born in 1945, he grew up with a pianist father who was a child drummer, 78s of Waller, Tatum and Shaw, and relatives who played the theater circuit.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I’m here for the Fillius Jazz Archive, in Cortland, New York with drummer and band leader Danny D’Imperio. Thanks for joining me.
You and I are only a few years apart, and I have some vivid memories of what grabbed me as a kid musically, and I’m wondering what grabbed you?

Well first of all my father, who was that man there, was a musician. And I was born on March 14, 1945 in Sydney, New York, and we lived in Unadilla, New York. And he quit playing. At that time he was four years old, that was on the centerfold of the New York Times along with Crown Prince Hirohito, who was 16 years old. I’ve got the original newspaper upstairs. It’s just barely holding together. But he quit playing drums when he was about five. I mean you can see by those drums, I mean with that gooseneck hanging down. Actually it’s hard to see but there actually is a cymbal that’s attached to the bass drum pedal. They didn’t have high-hat cymbals in those days and so like when you hit the drum the cymbal would also hit the drum with the bass drum beater. I’d love to have that set of drums but I don’t know whatever happened to it. But anyway, he quit playing drums shortly thereafter. And around the age of 12 or 13 he contracted rheumatic fever and stayed home from school for one year as a result, and learned how to play the piano. So when I was born he worked for the War Department, he couldn’t get in the service at that time because of the rheumatic heart, so he worked for the War Department, and played piano on the side. So my first recollections when we lived in Unadilla, New York on the coffee table in the living room were the old 78 albums, which you open them up and there’d be four or five 78’s in it, and there’d be Fats Waller and Art Tatum, and people like that, Artie Shaw, you know, all of the famous guys at the time. And I got kind of attracted to that. I said, like they’d put them on the record player and I’d rock, like I’m rocking now, I rocked so much in my crib upstairs in my bedroom that I actually (and I’ve got the scar to this day) rocked my crib into the hallway and the whole crib came right down the stairs and my mother and father thought I was dead. there, I’ll tell you about the other one which I got later on. But I was always rocking. I just always loved to rock. Even in a car, even in a straight chair I rock. I don’t know why but I do. But the music was always in the house. And my uncle was a bass player, my grandfather — who lived to be 100 — was a violin player and a shoemaker, and his wife, my grandmother, my father’s mother, was a pianist — not a jazz pianist but a pianist, and they played the theater circuit with this fascination of a 4-year-old drummer, and they ended up playing the Hippodrome Theater in New York City with Baby Rose Marie, who was later on I believe “The Dick Van Dyke Show,” Rose Marie. And she was on the bill as well in the Hippodrome Theater. So that was the way that started. But my fascination came from the musical part of my family.
